name: Rangpur
tagline: Tajhat's palace, Carmichael's red brick, and the village where Begum Rokeya was born.

guide.bestTime: October to March (cool, dry) — May–July for Haribhanga mango season
guide.gettingThere: By train to Rangpur railway station, by road from Dhaka (~7–8 hr) and Bogura (~3 hr), or by plane to Saidpur airport (~50 km north). Rangpur is the divisional headquarters and the gateway to all eight northern districts.
guide.difficulty: Easy — flat terrain, a working divisional city with good hotels and a compact heritage core.

mustVisit.name: Tajhat Palace (Rangpur Museum)
mustVisit.description: The grand neoclassical palace of the Tajhat zamindars on the southern edge of Rangpur city — broad marble stairs, a long arcaded façade and now the Rangpur Museum holding Pala-era sculpture and regional antiquities.
mustVisit.history: Built in the early 20th century by Maharaja Kumar Gopal Lal Roy, a Sikh zamindar whose family had migrated from Punjab. The two-storey palace is shaped like a crown ('taj') and was acquired by the government after independence; the Department of Archaeology now operates the Rangpur Museum here.

practical.hours: ~10 am – 5 pm; closed one weekly day

howToReach.fromDistrictTown: About 3 km south of Rangpur city centre at Tajhat
howToReach.transport: Rickshaw, CNG or easybike from town

tips: The Pala-era stone sculpture in the museum is the highlight inside
The marble staircase photographs best in the morning

mustVisit.name: Carmichael College
mustVisit.description: One of the country's grand colonial college campuses — long red-brick wings, a handsome clocktower, shady avenues and broad lawns, all still in active academic use.
mustVisit.history: Established in 1916 and named after Lord Carmichael, the then Governor of Bengal. For a century it has been one of north Bengal's most important seats of higher learning.

howToReach.fromDistrictTown: About 2 km west of the city centre

tips: It is a working college — be respectful in academic blocks
Walk the back lawns and look up at the clocktower

mustVisit.name: Begum Rokeya Memorial Centre, Payrabondh (Mithapukur)
mustVisit.description: The birthplace of Begum Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain — pioneer of women's education in Bengal — at Payrabondh village in Mithapukur, now a memorial centre with her family home, a small museum and gardens.
mustVisit.history: Rokeya was born here on 9 December 1880 to a Persian-Bengali Muslim aristocratic family whose ancestors had migrated from Tabriz. The memorial centre commemorates her life and her landmark works 'Sultana's Dream' and 'Padmarag', the schools she founded in Bhagalpur and Kolkata, and her broader role as the founder of women's education for Bengali Muslim women.

practical.hours: ~9 am – 5 pm; busiest on 9 December (her birth anniversary / Rokeya Day)

howToReach.fromDistrictTown: About 25 km south of Rangpur city in Payrabondh village, Mithapukur Upazila
howToReach.transport: Bus or CNG to Mithapukur, then easybike to Payrabondh

mustVisit.bestTime: 9 December (Rokeya Day) or any cool-month morning
tips: Read 'Sultana's Dream' before visiting — it makes the small museum read very differently
Pair with Mithapukur Mosque on the same morning

mustVisit.name: Mithapukur Mosque
mustVisit.description: A small, beautifully proportioned late-Mughal brick mosque in Mithapukur — three domes with the central one raised, four octagonal corner minarets, and terracotta floral and vine motifs around the three mihrabs.
mustVisit.history: Built in 1802 CE (1217 AH) by Sheikh Mohammad Asar, son of Sheikh Mohammad Saber. The compact 11.58 × 4.42 metre prayer hall is one of the best surviving examples of late-Mughal mosque architecture in northern Bangladesh, and is protected by the Department of Archaeology.

practical.hours: Open during five daily prayers; visitors welcome outside prayer times

howToReach.fromDistrictTown: About 22 km south of Rangpur city in Mithapukur Upazila

mustVisit.bestTime: Outside Friday noon prayers; morning light
tips: Cover head if female; remove shoes
The terracotta mihrab carvings are the highlight — look closely

mustVisit.name: Itakumari Rajbari (Pirgacha)
mustVisit.description: The arched, vine-grown ruins of an 18th-century zamindar estate in Pirgacha — broken halls, an old tank and a temple foundation, all slowly being reclaimed by the trees.
mustVisit.history: Seat of an old north-Bengal zamindar family whose estate dates to the 18th century. The buildings have been ruined for generations; today the site is more atmosphere than architecture, but the scale of the masonry still reads.

howToReach.fromDistrictTown: About 35 km east of Rangpur city in Pirgacha Upazila
howToReach.transport: Bus or CNG to Pirgacha, then easybike to Itakumari

tips: Wear closed shoes — the brush is dense
Bring water; there are no shops at the ruin itself

mustVisit.name: Vinno Jagat Amusement & Cultural Park
mustVisit.description: A large family amusement and cultural park on the north-western edge of Rangpur city — rides, gardens, a small zoo and themed cultural sets, the popular weekend day-out of the divisional capital.

howToReach.fromDistrictTown: About 15 km north-west of Rangpur city on the Taraganj road
howToReach.transport: Car, CNG or easybike from city

tips: Busy on holidays — go early for the rides
Pair with a Haribhanga mango orchard visit in summer

specialties.name: Haribhanga Mango
specialties.description: Rangpur's signature mango — fibreless, fleshy, very sweet, with a small seed. Grown mainly in Mithapukur, Badarganj, Pirganj and Sadar upazilas, and a key part of the district's June–July economy.

specialties.name: Pelka
specialties.description: The earthy north-Bengal greens-and-kalai-flour curry — a Rangpur-division home-cooking tradition that you'll find on every serious north-Bengal menu.

specialties.name: Kalai Ruti & Sidol Bhorta
specialties.description: Thick gram-flour rotis served hot with pungent fermented-fish sidol bhorta, mashed eggplant, or country-chicken curry — the standard north-Bengal breakfast plate.
specialties.venue: Kalai Ghor & roadside dhabas, Rangpur city

specialties.name: Rokeya Day
specialties.description: Every 9 December the country marks Begum Rokeya's birth anniversary — Rangpur sees the largest gathering, with seminars, school programmes and a heavy flow of visitors to Payrabondh.

bucketlist.title: Stand on the marble stairs of Tajhat Palace
bucketlist.detail: An early-20th-century neoclassical palace shaped like a crown, built by a Punjabi-origin Sikh zamindar — now the Rangpur Museum, with Pala-era stone sculpture inside.
bucketlist.whereOrHow: Tajhat, southern edge of Rangpur city

bucketlist.title: Walk the avenues of Carmichael College
bucketlist.detail: Long red-brick wings, a handsome clocktower and broad shady lawns — one of the country's grand colonial college campuses, in active academic use since 1916.
bucketlist.whereOrHow: Carmichael College, west of city centre

bucketlist.title: Visit Begum Rokeya's home at Payrabondh
bucketlist.detail: Where the pioneer of women's education in Bengal — author of 'Sultana's Dream' — was born in 1880. Read her once before you go and the small museum at Payrabondh changes shape.

bucketlist.title: See the terracotta mihrabs of Mithapukur Mosque
bucketlist.detail: A small, beautifully proportioned late-Mughal three-domed mosque built in 1802 — its three mihrabs decorated with floral and vine terracotta motifs.

bucketlist.title: Explore the Itakumari Rajbari ruins
bucketlist.detail: Arched, vine-grown remains of an 18th-century zamindar estate — more atmosphere than architecture now, but the scale of the masonry still reads.

bucketlist.title: Eat a Haribhanga mango at the orchard
bucketlist.detail: Rangpur's signature mango — fibreless, fleshy, very sweet, with a small seed. At its best a few hours after the morning pluck.

bucketlist.title: Try pelka at a home-style canteen
bucketlist.detail: The earthy north-Bengal greens-and-kalai-flour curry — a Rangpur-division home tradition you cannot order south of here.

bucketlist.title: Eat kalai ruti with sidol bhorta
bucketlist.detail: Thick black-gram-and-rice-flour rotis with pungent fermented-fish sidol bhorta — the working breakfast of the Rangpur belt.
bucketlist.whereOrHow: Kalai Ghor & roadside dhabas, Rangpur city

bucketlist.title: Take a slow afternoon at Vinno Jagat
bucketlist.detail: Rides, gardens and themed cultural sets at the divisional capital's most popular family park — a slice of how Rangpur spends its weekends.

bucketlist.title: Buy aakher gur at a winter haat
bucketlist.detail: Sugarcane molasses pressed and boiled at village mills — the northern alternative to date-palm gur, used in winter pithas and tea.

bucketlist.title: Take a train through Rangpur Junction
bucketlist.detail: Rangpur is the working railhead of north-western Bangladesh — the platform's tea-stall life is a quiet study in itself.

bucketlist.title: Walk the city for the old mosques and tanks
bucketlist.detail: Beyond Mithapukur, the divisional city carries old mosques, tanks and zamindari fragments tucked into its modern streets — easiest at a slow morning pace.

foods.name: Haribhanga Mango
foods.description: Rangpur's signature mango — fibreless, fleshy, very sweet, small-seeded. Grown in Mithapukur, Badarganj and Pirganj.

foods.name: Pelka
foods.description: Earthy regional curry of greens cooked with small kalai-flour balls — a north-Bengal home-cooking staple.

foods.name: Kalai Ruti
foods.description: Thick rotis of black-gram and rice flour, served hot with sidol bhorta, mashed eggplant, or country-chicken curry.
foods.whereToFind: Kalai Ghor & roadside dhabas, Rangpur city

foods.name: Sidol Bhorta
foods.description: Pungent fermented-fish mash, pounded with red chili, onion and mustard oil — the classic partner to kalai ruti.

foods.name: Aakher Gur
foods.description: Sugarcane molasses pressed and boiled at village mills — used in winter pithas and to sweeten tea.

foods.name: Aakher Gur Pitha
foods.description: Winter rice pithas — chitoi and bhapa — drizzled with fresh sugarcane molasses.

foods.name: Teesta River Fish
foods.description: Fresh catch from the Teesta and Ghaghot — small carp and catfish in light mustard curries.

famousPeople.name: Begum Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain
famousPeople.knownFor: Pioneer of women's education in Bengal and one of the foundational feminist writers of the subcontinent. Born at Payrabondh in Mithapukur on 9 December 1880; author of 'Sultana's Dream' (1905) and 'Padmarag', founder of the Sakhawat Memorial Girls' School in Kolkata (1911). Her birth anniversary is observed nationally as Rokeya Day.

didYouKnow: Rangpur is the headquarters of Rangpur Division and one of the oldest district names in northern Bengal — a British district since 1772, though the modern Rangpur district in its current shape dates to 1 February 1984, after greater Rangpur was split into five.

Begum Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain — pioneer of women's education in Bengal and author of 'Sultana's Dream' — was born at Payrabondh in Mithapukur Upazila on 9 December 1880, observed nationally as Rokeya Day.
Tajhat Palace was built in the early 20th century by Maharaja Kumar Gopal Lal Roy, a Sikh zamindar whose family had migrated from Punjab — its plan is said to be shaped like a crown ('taj').
Carmichael College, founded in 1916 and named after the then Governor of Bengal, has been one of north Bengal's premier colleges for over a century.
Mithapukur Mosque was built in 1802 — a late-Mughal three-domed brick mosque with terracotta floral motifs around its mihrabs, protected by the Department of Archaeology.
The Haribhanga mango — fibreless, fleshy, sweet — is Rangpur's branded fruit, with most of the country's orchards in Mithapukur, Badarganj and Pirganj.
